catalog_quote: 4. Stress In all four languages stress is contrastive and thus phonemic. Examples of contrastive stress are as follows: [...] Miani /'un̯u/ 'ripe' /u'n̯u/ 'red' /ga'gat̯oƀ/ 'to take it down' /'gagat̯oƀ/ 'to look at' /'uřam/ 'his stomach' /u'řam/ 'basket' [...] An interesting feature of stress has been noted in comparing two syllable words that are similar in all four languages. new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (25-pp. scan, no text layer; the PDF's metadata: Acrobat Paper Capture 2005) and rendered PDF pp. 1, 11, 12 to PNG and read the page images. Page 11 (running head 'Maiani, Miani, Mala and Maia 11') carries the heading '4. Stress' and the sentence 'In all four languages stress is contrastive and thus phonemic. Examples of contrastive stress are as follows:' followed by the Maiani pairs; page 12 (running head '12 Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages') carries the Miani block /'uŋu/ 'ripe' / /u'ŋu/ 'red', /ga'gat̯ob̯/ 'to take it down' / /'gagat̯ob̯/ 'to look at', /'uřam/ 'his stomach' / /u'řam/ 'basket', then Mala and Maia pairs, then the paragraph 'An interesting feature of stress…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is phonemic (contrastive) in Miani: word-level minimal pairs differ only in whether the first or second syllable is stressed (e.g. 'uŋu 'ripe' vs u'ŋu 'red'; 'gagatob 'to look at' vs ga'gatob 'to take it down'). No placement rule is given; the only generalisation is a cross-language observation that in comparable disyllables Miani (like Maiani and Mala) stresses the second syllable, whereas Maia stresses the first. The 1994 OPD repeats the same three pairs (spelled 'unu/u'nu, ga'gatow/'gagatow, 'uram/u'ram) and adds that phonemic stress is not.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; the second-syllable pattern is offered as a tendency in disyllables, not a rule, and the minimal pairs show both first- and second-syllable stress. One pair ('uřam 'his stomach' vs u'řam 'basket') is plausibly morphological (u- 'his' prefix), as in sister language Maia where person prefixes carry stress contrasts.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in a phonology/orthography sketch (isolated words); the OPD's allophony note refers to 'unstressed syllables' within the word. No phrase-level or intonation statement; no tone or length contrast reported.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Miani proper [pla] = Z'graggen's 'Tani' northern part (OPD title: 'Miani (Tani, Miani North)'; villages Yoro, Suwat, Mugumat). May & Loeweke's Miani examples come from main-dialect speakers (Andrew Gai, Jacob Kulilain); they note a small coastal Miani dialect differing in consonants (/d/, /l/ for main-dialect /ʒ/) but say nothing about its stress. The OPD's running header reads 'Miani (Pila, Coastal Maia) OPD', a template artifact - the title page, villages and data are Miani. Sister variety Maiani [tnh] (maia1253, 'Miani South') is covered by the same 1985 paper (Maiani pairs 'apa/a'pa) but is a separate Glottolog language.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the source of the existing statement (lexical/unpredictable, contrastive stress); the full passage confirms it and adds the second-syllable tendency in disyllables, which the existing statement's truncated quote only begins ('An interesting feature of stress has been noted in co'). The catalog record for Miani has an empty rule field; this work supplies 'contrastive, unpredictable; disyllables tend to second-syllable stress'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress in Miani is contrastive (phonemic): three minimal pairs differ only in initial vs. second-syllable stress, so placement is not predictable from the segmental string; the only generalisation offered is a tendency in disyllabic cognate words for Miani (with Maiani and Mala) to stress the second syllable where Maia stresses the first. Stress is not written in the recommended orthography. (In the PDF image the t of /ga'gatob/ carries a dental diacritic and the final b is barred; the r of /'uřam/ has a haček.)
new_statements.exceptions: No exceptions stated; the second-syllable tendency is explicitly a 'tends to' observation on two-syllable cognates, and the minimal pairs show both positions. Section 2.4.2 (p. 6) adds that the vibrant is a flap between vowels in unstressed syllables; 5.3 (pp. 13-14) records speaker proposals to mark stress (preceding h, doubled consonant), neither adopted.
new_statements.identity_note: Work 0 (May 1994 OPD 'Maiani (Tani, Miani South) [TNH]') describes Maiani, glottocode maia1253, not Miani [pla] = 'Tani, Miani North' (Z'graggen's 'Tani' covers both; the 1985 paper p. 1: 'Tani = Miani and Maiani'). The 1985 paper treats four languages (Maiani, Miani, Mala, Maia) with separate Miani examples on p. 12; the authors lived in a Maiani village. No dialect of Miani is named in any opened source.
